# Intermediate-Risk Pulmonary Embolism in 2026

By [Hassan Bencheqroun, MD, EMBA](/author/hassan-bencheqroun-md-emba) - Last Updated: April 20, 2026

## *New guidelines, new evidence, and the same old problem*

The 2026 American Heart Association (AHA)/American College of Cardiology (ACC)/ American College of Clinical Pharmacy/American College of Emergency Physicians/ American College of Chest Physicians/Society for Cardiovascular Angiography & Interventions/Society of Hospital Medicine/Society of Interventional Radiology/Society for Vascular Medicine/Society of Vascular Nursing guideline for acute pulmonary embolism (PE) is the most ambitious attempt in years to standardize how we think about, classify, and treat PE. It retired the terms *massive* and *submassive*, introduced a five-tier clinical category system (A through E), and added a respiratory modifier. The HI-PEITHO trial, published simultaneously in the *New England Journal of Medicine* and presented at ACC 2026, offered the first evidence from a randomized controlled trial (RCT) that catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT) reduces a composite clinical end point in intermediate-risk PE.

These are real advances. But after spending time with the guideline document, the trial data, and the firestorm of commentary that followed, I think we need an honest conversation about what these developments actually deliver at the bedside and where they fall short.

To ground this discussion, start with the [new framework](https://www.ahajournals.org/cms/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001415/asset/dd9dbb7b-03a9-4bf2-b6ba-e9aded72e43a/assets/graphic/cir.0000000000001415.fig02.jpg), then meet a patient I could have seen last week on any tele-ICU shift in America.

### **Clinical Vignette**

#### ***The Patient***

A 71-year-old woman with a history of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF; baseline EF, 58%), hypertension, obesity (BMI, 38), and recent left knee arthroplasty presents to the emergency department 10 days post-surgery with progressive dyspnea over 48 hours. She is alert, mildly diaphoretic, speaking in short sentences.

**Vital signs on arrival:** Heart rate (HR), 112 bpm; respiratory rate, 26 breaths/min; BP, 104/72 mm Hg (mean arterial pressure [MAP], 83 mm Hg); oxygen saturation measured by pulse oximetry (SpO2), 89% on room air, improving to 93% on 4 L of oxygen via nasal cannula. Temperature is 37.2° C.

**Laboratory values:** Troponin I, 0.18 ng/mL (elevated); B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), 580 pg/mL (her baseline from a clinic visit 3 months ago was 420 pg/mL); lactate, 2.8 mmol/L; creatinine, 1.4 mg/dL (baseline, 1.0).

**CT pulmonary angiography:** Bilateral pulmonary emboli involving the right main and left lower lobar arteries. The right ventricle to left ventricle ratio (RV:LV) is 1.3 on CT. No evidence of right heart thrombus in transit.

She begins receiving unfractionated heparin. Forty-five minutes later, her systolic BP drops to 87 mm Hg for approximately 45 seconds during a coughing spell, then recovers to 98/68 (MAP, 78) without intervention. Fifteen minutes after that, an automated cuff reads 92/58 (MAP, 69). The nurse rechecks manually: BP is 102/70 (MAP, 81).

#### ***Now Apply the 2026 AHA/ACC Guideline***

This is the patient who exposes every fault line in the new classification. Watch what happens when you try to categorize her condition.

***The Four Criticisms, Alive in One Patient***

**Criticism 1 (Score interchangeability):** Her Simplified Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (sPESI) is 2 (age >80 receives 0 points, but she scores 2 for cancer-free; HR, >110; SpO2 <90%; systolic BP [SBP] preserved). This places her in Category C. Her Bova score is 3 (HR, 100-109 = 0; SBP > 100 = 0; RV dysfunction = 2; troponin = 1). A Bova score of 4 or lower places her in Category B. Same patient. Two different risk tiers. The guideline permits either tool, and the clinical path diverges based on which one you pick.

**Criticism 2 (BNP-troponin conflation):** Her BNP of 580 pg/mL is flagged as a positive cardiac biomarker. But her baseline BNP was 420, a 38% increase that could easily reflect volume shifts post-surgery in a patient with HFpEF. Her troponin, at 0.18 ng/mL, is genuinely elevated and more likely reflects acute RV myocardial injury from the PE. The guideline treats these two markers as interchangeable. They are not. If a clinician anchors on the BNP value alone, this patient looks like C3 even without meaningful acute RV injury. If a clinician correctly prioritizes the troponin, the classification is the same (C3), but the reasoning is fundamentally different, and the confidence in the assessment changes.

**Criticism 3 (Transient SBP < 90):** The 45-second dip to 87 mm Hg during a coughing spell technically meets the D1 criterion: transient SBP less than 90. That single reading, captured by an automated cuff during a Valsalva-equivalent maneuver, now reclassifies her from C3 to D1 and implies she may need consideration for advanced therapy. The clinical reality is that her hemodynamics recovered spontaneously, and SBP was never sustained below 90.

**Criticism 4 (MAP < 60 as normotensive shock):** The automated cuff that read 92/58 produces a calculated MAP of 69, above the D2 threshold. But the manual recheck reading was 102/70, with MAP of 81. Had the nurse not rechecked, and had a different automated reading landed at MAP 58, this patient would meet the D2 “normotensive shock” criterion: a MAP below 60 in a patient whose SBP was never sustained below 90. The guideline calls this *normotensive*. It is not.

#### ***What Physiology Actually Tells Us: Echocardiography and VExUS at the Bedside***

Here is where the guideline stops and where the bedside clinician needs to keep going. Scores and biomarkers have told us this patient is somewhere between Categories B and D1, depending on which tool you use and which BP reading you believe. That range is clinically meaningless for decision-making.

A focused echocardiogram and venous Doppler assessment (venous excess ultrasound score [VExUS]) performed at the bedside within 20 minutes of admission tells a different story entirely.

The echocardiographic findings are unambiguous. An RV outflow tract velocity time integral (RVOT-VTI) of 7.8 cm and LV outflow tract velocity time integral (LVOT-VTI) of 11.2 cm confirm that this patient has a critically reduced cardiac output. The tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE) of 12 mm reflects severe RV systolic dysfunction. The McConnell sign localizes the insult to acute pressure overload, not chronic cardiomyopathy. These findings go far beyond the binary “RV dilated, yes or no” that the guideline relies on.

The VExUS assessment adds a dimension the guideline does not even contemplate. The dilated, noncollapsible inferior vena cava (IVC) tells you central venous pressure is elevated, but that alone is nonspecific. What transforms the assessment is the Doppler interrogation of the hepatic, portal, and intrarenal veins. Systolic flow reversal in the hepatic vein, a pulsatile portal vein with a pulsatility index above 50%, and discontinuous intrarenal venous flow together constitute a VExUS grade 3 pattern: severe venous congestion with end-organ impact.

This is the hemodynamic signature of a patient in whom RV failure has caused backward congestion that is reaching the kidneys and the liver. Her creatinine is already rising. Her lactate is 2.8 mmol/L. Her BP is 102/70. She looks stable. She is not.

#### ***The Clinical Decision***

This patient is in compensated obstructive shock. Her systemic vascular resistance is maintaining her BP at the cost of tissue perfusion. The LVOT-VTI of 11.2 cm translates to a cardiac output that is incompatible with sustained end-organ viability. The VExUS pattern confirms that the congestion is not theoretical; it is already injuring organs.

No composite score told us this. No single biomarker told us this. The guideline classification placed her somewhere between Categories B and D1, depending on the clinician. The ultrasound probe placed her exactly where she is: in shock, with a narrow window before decompensation becomes irreversible.

This is the patient who fits the HI-PEITHO phenotype: RV strain, elevated troponin, physiologic stress, and now objective evidence of low cardiac output and end-organ congestion determined by ultrasonography. In a center with Pulmonary Embolism Response Team (PERT) capability and catheter-lab readiness, this is the patient for whom early CDT (or mechanical thrombectomy if thrombolytic therapy is contraindicated) should be on the operating table, discussed as a team, and acted on within hours, not as a rescue after she codes.

### The New Classification: Ambition Without Simplicity

The vignette provided here is not an edge case. It is an every-night case for anyone covering an ICU or a tele-ICU panel. The old language was clumsy. “Submassive” PE meant different things to different clinicians and lumped together patients with wildly different risk profiles. The [new A through E system](https://www.ahajournals.org/cms/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001415/asset/553fcf76-8304-47f0-855a-f3f423c45140/assets/graphic/cir.0000000000001415.fig03.jpg) tries to fix this by anchoring classification to validated severity scores (sPESI, PESI, Bova score), biomarker status (troponin, BNP), imaging (RV dysfunction on CT or echocardiography), and hemodynamic parameters.

In theory, this is progress. In practice, the framework introduces a level of complexity that does not translate into clearer decision-making. Category C alone has three subcategories (C1, C2, C3), each with a respiratory modifier (R). Category D has two subcategories with the same modifier. A physician standing at the bedside of a sick patient now has to mentally navigate a branching algorithm that, at its core, still does not answer the question that matters most: Is this patient in shock?

The critique by **Josh Farkas, MD,** on PulmCrit/EMCrit identified the four problems that our vignette brought to life: score interchangeability at the B/C boundary, BNP-troponin conflation, the transient SBP trigger for D1, and the MAP below 60 self-contradiction in the normotensive shock definition. These are not theoretical objections. They produce different treatment trajectories for the same patient in the same emergency department on the same night.

### The Real Problem: We Still Aren’t Measuring Shock

My colleague **Rory Spiegel, MD,** has been making this point for years, and the 2026 guideline proves him right: we are still not measuring shock. My most fundamental concern with this document is that, despite its ambition, it does not provide a practical strategy for identifying shock at the bedside. The tools it recommends—sPESI, PESI, Hestia criteria—are disposition scores. They were designed to identify which patients can safely go home. They were not designed to evaluate real-time hemodynamics, and they should not be repurposed for that task.

What is actually happening in the patient with hemodynamically significant PE is a well-understood physiologic process. As RV failure reduces cardiac output, systemic vascular resistance rises to compensate. Blood pressure is temporarily preserved while tissue perfusion collapses. The macrocirculation and microcirculation uncouple. These patients are in true shock. Not “pre-shock.” Not “normotensive shock.” Not a special subtype. Shock.

Our vignette demonstrated this with precision. The BP was 102/70 mm Hg. The LVOT-VTI was 11.2 cm. The VExUS pattern showed grade 3 venous congestion reaching the kidneys. That is the dissociation between macro-hemodynamics and tissue perfusion that the guideline fails to capture with its score-based approach.

If we want to risk-stratify PE appropriately, we need to move toward physiology and away from score-based abstraction. That means rigorous echocardiographic assessment: RVOT-VTI below 9.5 cm and LVOT-VTI at or below 15 cm as markers of reduced cardiac output, TAPSE for RV systolic function, and McConnell sign for acuity. It means a VExUS protocol: IVC assessment followed by hepatic, portal, and intrarenal venous Doppler echocardiography to quantify the downstream impact of RV failure on end-organ perfusion. And it means a careful physical examination: assessment of mottling, capillary refill, urine output trends, and mental status.

### HI-PEITHO: What the Data Actually Show

Against this backdrop, the HI-PEITHO trial offers the first RCT evidence for CDT in intermediate-risk PE. The trial screened more than 4,300 patients at 59 centers. Only 544 were randomized—roughly 13% of those screened. The enrolled population represented a narrow phenotype: patients with RV strain, elevated troponin, and at least two signs of physiologic stress. The average National Early Warning Score (NEWS) was 6.

The trial met its primary composite end point: PE-related death, cardiopulmonary decompensation or collapse, or recurrence of PE. The relative risk reduction was 61%. That is the headline.

Here is what is behind it. Pulmonary embolism–related death was rare in both groups and numerically similar (0.4% CDT vs 1.1% anticoagulation). Cardiac arrest was numerically similar (1.5% vs 2.2%). Intubation was numerically similar (1.8% vs 2.2%). Recurrent PE was identical (0.4% vs 0.4%). None of these hard end points drove the result.

What drove the composite was the NEWS. Only two patients in the CDT arm (0.7%) experienced a NEWS of 9 or above within 7 days, compared with 19 (7%) in the anticoagulation arm. The manuscript labels this “cardiopulmonary decompensation or collapse,” bundling a transient worsening of vital signs with cardiac arrest and intubation under a single umbrella term. The supplementary appendix reveals that the NEWS component drove the entire difference.

The crossover problem compounds this. The trial permitted rescue CDT in the anticoagulation arm. More patients in the anticoagulation group (9.2%) crossed over compared with patients in the intervention group (2.9%). Nearly all crossovers were triggered by a rising NEWS, not by vasopressor dependence or cardiac arrest. We cannot know whether those deteriorations were transient or would have led to hard outcomes. Major bleeding as determined by International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis criteria was approximately double in the CDT group (4% vs 2%), although not statistically significant.

For our vignette patient, HI-PEITHO is relevant but not dispositive. She fits the trial phenotype. CDT would be a reasonable option discussed through PERT. But the decision to intervene should not rest on a composite end point driven by NEWS. It should rest on the echocardiographic and VExUS evidence of shock physiology that the guideline does not incorporate.

### Putting It Together: What Should Clinicians Do Now?

For the majority of patients with intermediate-risk PE, anticoagulation remains the right treatment. For the narrow subset with objective evidence of RV strain, positive troponin, and clinical signs of physiologic stress, CDT now has RCT evidence supporting its use. Mechanical thrombectomy remains an option when thrombolytics are contraindicated. Trials comparing thrombectomy with anticoagulation for intermediate-risk PE (PEERLESS, PE-TRACT, STORM-PE) are ongoing.

The role of the PERT cannot be overstated. High-volume centers report that only 10% to 15% of patients with intermediate- to high-risk PE ultimately receive invasive therapy. That proportion reflects appropriate patient selection.

### A Simpler Framework

My colleague Dr. Rory Spiegel has argued, and I agree, that rather than the elaborate A through E system, what clinicians need at the bedside can be distilled into four tiers. The framework below draws on his thinking and on the physiologic approach outlined above.

This is not a replacement for the guideline. It is a translation. The nuance lives in identifying which patients with intermediate-risk PE are actually in shock, compensated or otherwise. Our vignette patient belongs in the last row, not because her BP was ever sustained below 90 but because her LVOT-VTI was 11.2 cm and her kidneys were congested. That determination requires physiology, not scores.

### Where We Go From Here

Several ongoing trials will shape the next iteration of this debate. PEITHO-3 is testing reduced-dose systemic alteplase. PEERLESS and PEERLESS-II compare mechanical thrombectomy with CDT or anticoagulation. PE-TRACT and STORM-PE examine catheter-based interventions versus anticoagulation alone.

In the meantime, the field needs to invest in better bedside tools. Point-of-care echocardiography protocols that go beyond “RV dilated or not” toward quantitative cardiac output assessment would be transformative. VExUS as a systematic evaluation of venous congestion and end-organ impact in acute PE deserves prospective study. These tools exist. They are teachable. They are available at 3 AM. What is missing is a guideline that tells clinicians to use them.

We also need to be honest about the role of industry. HI-PEITHO was funded by Boston Scientific. The investigators disclosed significant financial relationships. That does not invalidate the data, but it does mean we should read the manuscript with the same rigor we would apply to any industry-funded trial. The composite end point was met. The hard end points were not. Both facts matter.

### A Question for Part 2: The Ethics of What Comes Next

HI-PEITHO opens a question this article cannot fully answer, and one I intend to address later in *Pulmonology Today*. After a positive randomized trial showing a 61% relative risk reduction with CDT for intermediate to high-risk PE, do we still have equipoise? For the HI-PEITHO phenotype (Categories C3 through D2), the answer is no longer straightforward. For the broader intermediate-risk population (Categories C1 and C2), equipoise is preserved. For mechanical thrombectomy, no RCT data exist at all. These distinctions matter enormously for trial design, for institutional review boards, and most importantly, for the patients we ask to enroll. What do we tell a patient like the one in our clinical vignette, who fits the HI-PEITHO profile, when we ask her to accept a chance of being randomly assigned to anticoagulation alone? What does the Declaration of Helsinki require of us when a published *New England Journal of Medicine* trial found the comparator arm inferior? And for sponsors designing trials with novel investigational products for intermediate-risk PE, is a blanket anticoagulation-alone control arm still ethically defensible across all categories? These are not abstract questions. They will shape every PE trial protocol written in the next 5 years. More on this in Part 2.

### Take-Home for *Pulmonology Today* Readers

1. **The 2026 AHA/ACC PE guideline retires the terms *massive* and *submassive* in favor of a five-tier A through E classification.** The new system is more granular but introduces clinically significant ambiguities at the B/C and C/D boundaries that can produce different treatment paths for the same patient.
2. **Four specific flaws in the classification deserve scrutiny:** interchangeable use of sPESI, PESI, and Bova for risk-tier assignment; conflation of BNP with troponin as equivalent biomarkers; a transient SBP threshold of less than 90 mm Hg that is too sensitive; and a “normotensive shock” definition that includes frank hypotension (MAP, <60).
3. **The guideline still lacks a practical strategy for identifying compensated obstructive shock.** Disposition scores (sPESI, PESI, Hestia criteria) were not built for hemodynamic assessment. Patients with preserved BP but failing tissue perfusion remain the hardest to classify and the most dangerous to miss.
4. **Bedside echocardiography and VExUS should be part of the workup for any patient with intermediate-risk PE.** RVOT-VTI of less than 9.5 cm and LVOT-VTI of 15 cm or less identify low cardiac output. TAPSE quantifies RV systolic function. Hepatic, portal, and intrarenal venous Doppler ultrasonography (VExUS) detect end-organ congestion before it appears in laboratory values. These tools are available and teachable, and they change management.
5. **HI-PEITHO provides the first RCT evidence for use of CDT for intermediate- to high-risk PE.** The 61% relative risk reduction in the composite end point is real, but it was driven by a physiologic surrogate (NEWS ≥9), not by mortality, cardiac arrest, or intubation. Read the supplementary appendix.
6. **CDT is not for all intermediate-risk PEs.** Only 13% of screened patients in HI-PEITHO were enrolled. The benefit applies to a narrow phenotype: RV strain, positive troponin, and at least two signs of physiologic stress. Most patients with intermediate-risk PE do well with anticoagulation alone.
7. **Mechanical thrombectomy has no RCT evidence in intermediate-risk PE.** PEERLESS, PE-TRACT, and STORM-PE are ongoing. Until those data arrive, thrombectomy remains an option for patients for whom thromoblytics are contraindicated, not a first-line intervention.
8. **PERT activation should be the standard for any patient with an intermediate- to high-risk PE.** High-volume centers report that only 10% to 15% of these patients ultimately receive invasive therapy. Multidisciplinary decision-making is the safeguard against both undertreatment and overtreatment.
9. **A simpler, physiology-driven framework** (as proposed by Dr. Rory Spiegel and outlined in this article) **can replace the A through E complexity at the bedside:** very low risk (discharge), low risk (anticoagulation, hospital admission), intermediate risk (anticoagulation, monitored setting, echocardiography/VExUS, PERT), and high-risk/shock (reperfusion plus ICU). The critical step is identifying which patients with intermediate-risk PE are actually in shock.
10. **The ethics of future PE trials have shifted.** After HI-PEITHO, equipoise in the C3-D2 phenotype is strained. Trial designers, institutional review boards, and investigators will need to grapple with what constitutes an acceptable control arm for the patients who match the HI-PEITHO profile. Part 2 of this series will address this in depth.

**Coming in Part 2:** The next article in this series will address the ethics of clinical equipoise after HI-PEITHO, informed consent in PE device trials, and what trial sponsors owe patients when the evidence base shifts mid-program.

results.content:
You obtain a CT which reveals large bilateral pulmonary emboli. A bedside echocardiogram shows right ventricular dilation and hypokinesis, and her troponin returns mildly elevated. Despite these findings, she remains normotensive. Traditionally, these patients are treated with anticoagulation alone, with escalation to thrombolysis reserved for hemodynamic collapse. However, over the past several years your hospital has increasingly involved the Pulmonary Embolism Response Team (PERT) for patients like this, with consideration of mechanical thrombectomy and catheter-directed thrombolysis. [...] 2026;153(1):21-34. [Answer Key].

  

Bottom Line

While anticoagulation remains the mainstay of treatment for acute pulmonary embolism (PE), several relatively new therapies are available to assist in management, particularly in cases where clot burden and location lead to strain on the right heart. These alternative therapies include surgical thrombectomy, catheter-based mechanical thrombectomy, and catheter-directed thrombolysis. Many institutions have now implemented PE response teams (PERT), multidisciplinary teams designed to evaluate patients on a case-by-case basis and make recommendations regarding optimal therapy. Several recent studies have evaluated not only the individual treatment options, but also the utility of PERT in general. [...] The Ultrasound Assisted Thrombolysis of Pulmonary Embolism (ULTIMA) trialwas a randomized, multicenter trial comparing ultrasound-assisted catheter-directed thrombolysis (USAT) to anticoagulation alone in intermediate-risk PE. USAT led to a substantially greater reduction in RV/LV ratio (mean decrease of 0.30 ± 0.20) compared with heparin alone (0.03 ± 0.16; P < 0.001), along with significant improvements in other right heart echocardiographic parameters, without differences in major bleeding, hemodynamic decompensation, or recurrent VTE at 90 days. This study unfortunately involved a very small sample size (59 patients) and focused on a short-term surrogate outcomesrather than patient-centered measuressuch as development of CTEPH or quality of life.

# Management of Intermediate-Risk PE

By [Sang](https://emergencymedicine.wustl.edu/author/nsang/) • April 7, 2026 April 7, 2026

Washington University Emergency Medicine Journal Club – March 19th, 2026

**Dr. Brian Cohn**

Hey all,

This month’s journal club will look at the management of intermediate-risk PE, specifically evaluating PERT team activation, catheter-directed thrombolysis, and mechanical thrombectomy.

The PGY-1, PGY-2, and PGY-4 papers will be appraised using the Therapy form, while the PGY-3 paper will be appraised using the Meta-analysis form.

* * *

**Vignette**

You’re working one evening shift in TCC when EMS brings in a 64-year-old woman with shortness of breath and near-syncope. She reports that her symptoms began earlier that morning and have progressively worsened. She denies chest pain but feels markedly dyspneic with minimal exertion. Her past medical history is notable for hypertension and a recent knee replacement three weeks ago. Her vital signs show a heart rate of 118 bpm, blood pressure of 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate of 24, and oxygen saturation of 92% on room air. She appears uncomfortable but is speaking in full sentences. Her exam is notable for mild tachypnea but clear lungs and no signs of heart failure.

You obtain a CT which reveals large bilateral pulmonary emboli. A bedside echocardiogram shows right ventricular dilation and hypokinesis, and her troponin returns mildly elevated. Despite these findings, she remains normotensive. Traditionally, these patients are treated with anticoagulation alone, with escalation to thrombolysis reserved for hemodynamic collapse. However, over the past several years your hospital has increasingly involved the Pulmonary Embolism Response Team (PERT) for patients like this, with consideration of mechanical thrombectomy and catheter-directed thrombolysis.

Your patient is currently stable, but her imaging and biomarkers suggest a higher-risk PE. Should she receive anticoagulation alone, the traditional standard of care? Would catheter-directed thrombolysis reduce the risk of deterioration while avoiding the bleeding risk of systemic thrombolysis? Could mechanical thrombectomy rapidly reduce clot burden without the need for thrombolytics? And does activating a PERT team actually improve outcomes, or does it simply increase the use of invasive procedures? You decide to search the literature to see what evidence exists comparing anticoagulation alone, catheter-directed thrombolysis, mechanical thrombectomy, and multidisciplinary PERT activation for patients with intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism.

* * *

**PICO Question**

**Population:** In adult patients with intermediate-risk (submassive) pulmonary

embolism

**Intervention:** Does management with catheter-directed thrombolysis, mechanical

thrombectomy, or activation of a pulmonary embolism response team (PERT)

**Comparison:** Compared with treatment with anticoagulation alone

**Outcome:** Improve clinically meaningful outcomes such as mortality, hemodynamic

decompensation, recurrent PE, ICU utilization, or hospital length of stay?

**Bottom Line**

While [anticoagulation remains the mainstay of treatment](https://nam10.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.jacc.org%2Fdoi%2F10.1016%2Fj.jacc.2025.11.005%3Fgad_source%3D1%26gad_campaignid%3D23587533967%26gclid%3DCj0KCQjw1ZjOBhCmARIsADDuFTCX02344ILsiFfrL-Kllv9A0ySXNKBt_F5L-8Lnn10JfvZdjgHW5hIaAqGvEALw_wcB&data=05%7C02%7Cnsang%40wustl.edu%7C4789d2d14f0f4646aefe08de8d0a04aa%7C4ccca3b571cd4e6d974b4d9beb96c6d6%7C0%7C0%7C639103272193091310%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=pBNSGO1gJT8ZCoi0mO95GlDirmylL1FD2PCorcesUk8%3D&reserved=0) for acute pulmonary embolism (PE), several relatively new therapies are available to assist in management, particularly in cases where clot burden and location lead to strain on the right heart. These alternative therapies include [surgical thrombectomy](https://nam10.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fpmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov%2Farticles%2FPMC5579785%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cnsang%40wustl.edu%7C4789d2d14f0f4646aefe08de8d0a04aa%7C4ccca3b571cd4e6d974b4d9beb96c6d6%7C0%7C0%7C639103272193108655%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=8VY4TK7Pyitf9vpZWOX%2Fp%2BX3hOPIYPK2%2BqWdUyfanB0%3D&reserved=0), catheter-based [mechanical thrombectomy](https://nam10.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.ahajournals.org%2Fdoi%2F10.1161%2FCIRCINTERVENTIONS.122.012166&data=05%7C02%7Cnsang%40wustl.edu%7C4789d2d14f0f4646aefe08de8d0a04aa%7C4ccca3b571cd4e6d974b4d9beb96c6d6%7C0%7C0%7C639103272193119162%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=abE2tcqkYBMKFj0hBc91ZUIOYebQrWr3RsXJlKpcdN0%3D&reserved=0), and [catheter-directed thrombolysis](https://nam10.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov%2Fbooks%2FNBK536918%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cnsang%40wustl.edu%7C4789d2d14f0f4646aefe08de8d0a04aa%7C4ccca3b571cd4e6d974b4d9beb96c6d6%7C0%7C0%7C639103272193128389%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=0dAdxqP%2FeXTW1g6lbnaR3OLqFmR0Yyne8HaX15sf3ms%3D&reserved=0). Many institutions have now implemented [PE response teams (PERT)](https://nam10.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fpmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov%2Farticles%2FPMC9507552%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cnsang%40wustl.edu%7C4789d2d14f0f4646aefe08de8d0a04aa%7C4ccca3b571cd4e6d974b4d9beb96c6d6%7C0%7C0%7C639103272193137570%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=bQ5cLVElAQN239NF5zy1ajFlTZHArEdd1fm9j%2BZss%2B8%3D&reserved=0), multidisciplinary teams designed to evaluate patients on a case-by-case basis and make recommendations regarding optimal therapy. Several recent studies have evaluated not only the individual treatment options, but also the utility of PERT in general.

The [Ultrasound Assisted Thrombolysis of Pulmonary Embolism (ULTIMA) trial](https://nam10.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fpubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov%2F39470698%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cnsang%40wustl.edu%7C4789d2d14f0f4646aefe08de8d0a04aa%7C4ccca3b571cd4e6d974b4d9beb96c6d6%7C0%7C0%7C639103272193146480%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=G2bmZR4xmDAnZ4ArVA%2BrJjZfa9qBKGUlt93Dzu0WuWY%3D&reserved=0)was a randomized, multicenter trial comparing ultrasound-assisted catheter-directed thrombolysis (USAT) to anticoagulation alone in intermediate-risk PE. USAT led to a substantially greater reduction in RV/LV ratio (mean decrease of 0.30 ± 0.20) compared with heparin alone (0.03 ± 0.16; P < 0.001), along with significant improvements in other right heart echocardiographic parameters, without differences in major bleeding, hemodynamic decompensation, or recurrent VTE at 90 days. This study unfortunately involved a very small sample size (59 patients) and focused on a short-term [surrogate outcomes](https://nam10.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=http%3A%2F%2Fpmid.us%2F8815760&data=05%7C02%7Cnsang%40wustl.edu%7C4789d2d14f0f4646aefe08de8d0a04aa%7C4ccca3b571cd4e6d974b4d9beb96c6d6%7C0%7C0%7C639103272193155023%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=tEWAMr8VXHpPgG%2BKpFtxuMoigWDMi35G8Le10KHOmsg%3D&reserved=0)rather than [patient-centered measures](https://nam10.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fen.wikipedia.org%2Fwiki%2FPatient-centered_outcomes&data=05%7C02%7Cnsang%40wustl.edu%7C4789d2d14f0f4646aefe08de8d0a04aa%7C4ccca3b571cd4e6d974b4d9beb96c6d6%7C0%7C0%7C639103272193164624%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=7Z5%2BwKbjRUElR7cqGpqhrpYaB5598hd63Y6uaKUNZps%3D&reserved=0)such as development of CTEPH or quality of life.

The [STORM-PE trial](https://nam10.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fpubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov%2F41183181%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cnsang%40wustl.edu%7C4789d2d14f0f4646aefe08de8d0a04aa%7C4ccca3b571cd4e6d974b4d9beb96c6d6%7C0%7C0%7C639103272193173570%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=4lIl2FnglIF1IlJrOd%2BWyK5hhaOVpFdeXwRtWScI6GA%3D&reserved=0)was another international, randomized trial, this time comparing computer-assisted vacuum thrombectomy (CAVT) plus anticoagulation with anticoagulation alone in adults with intermediate-high–risk PE. The primary endpoint, change in RV/LV ratio at 48 hours, favored CAVT, with a mean reduction of 0.52±0.37 vs. 0.24±0.40 (between-group difference 0.27; 95% CI 0.12–0.43; P<0.001) and more CAVT patients achieved >0.2 reduction in RV/LV ratio. Safety outcomes were similar between groups: major adverse events within 7 days occurred in 4.3% vs 7.5%, major bleeding in 1 patient per group, and serious adverse events in 8.5% vs 15.1%. Key limitations include the small sample size (100 patients), open-label design with unblinded clinical assessments, and again the use of a short-term surrogate primary outcome (RV/LV ratio) rather than patient-centered endpoints leaving uncertainty about the true clinical benefit of CAVT.

The [PEERLESS trial](https://nam10.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fpubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov%2F24226805%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cnsang%40wustl.edu%7C4789d2d14f0f4646aefe08de8d0a04aa%7C4ccca3b571cd4e6d974b4d9beb96c6d6%7C0%7C0%7C639103272193182152%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=bhg9lVGU%2BwgMbUjThfOsDEJij6EUxKkZ%2FPvs%2F4A5%2Bm0%3D&reserved=0)was an international, multicenter, randomized controlled trial comparing large-bore mechanical thrombectomy (LBMT) with catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT) for intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism. The authors used a [hierarchical win ratio composite](https://nam10.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fjamanetwork.com%2Fjournals%2Fjama%2Farticle-abstract%2F2844500&data=05%7C02%7Cnsang%40wustl.edu%7C4789d2d14f0f4646aefe08de8d0a04aa%7C4ccca3b571cd4e6d974b4d9beb96c6d6%7C0%7C0%7C639103272193190622%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=rvcOAf57SNjWs3HkwoXNLX3BE%2Fd%2FnBjEJaDQ8Ptir3A%3D&reserved=0)of clinical outcomes (mortality, ICH, major bleeding, clinical deterioration/escalation, and ICU use) which strongly favored LBMT (win ratio of 5.01; 95% CI 3.68–6.97). This difference was primarily driven by a decrease in clinical deterioration/escalation (1.8% vs 5.4%) and markedly lower ICU use (41.6% vs 98.6%; ICU >24 hours 19.3% vs 64.5%). The latter was an inherently biased outcome, as most centers require ICU admission during catheter-directed thrombolytic infusion, [automatically biasing the results](https://nam10.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.acc.org%2Flatest-in-cardiology%2Farticles%2F2025%2F03%2F01%2F42%2Fperipheral-matters-putting-the-peerless-trial-in-perspective&data=05%7C02%7Cnsang%40wustl.edu%7C4789d2d14f0f4646aefe08de8d0a04aa%7C4ccca3b571cd4e6d974b4d9beb96c6d6%7C0%7C0%7C639103272193198841%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=CpgtRj1F4emJPSkSGwFQiRz54%2BwDS5OcFTz%2FJMwjBNk%3D&reserved=0)in favor of mechanical thrombectomy.There were no differences in rates of ICH or major bleeding and mortality was very low in both groups. It should also be noted that this was an [industry-funded study](https://nam10.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=http%3A%2F%2Finformahealthcare.com%2Fdoi%2Fpdf%2F10.1185%2F03007995.2011.628651&data=05%7C02%7Cnsang%40wustl.edu%7C4789d2d14f0f4646aefe08de8d0a04aa%7C4ccca3b571cd4e6d974b4d9beb96c6d6%7C0%7C0%7C639103272193207167%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=YQNdeVmc6DM4e%2BCLZbquP%2F9twpPsyJ%2FB4eo1lPhuv8U%3D&reserved=0)by the LBMT device manufacturer (Inari Medical).

Regarding the efficacy of PERT in general, [a systematic review and meta-analysis](https://nam10.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fpubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov%2F40258457%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cnsang%40wustl.edu%7C4789d2d14f0f4646aefe08de8d0a04aa%7C4ccca3b571cd4e6d974b4d9beb96c6d6%7C0%7C0%7C639103272193215850%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=R9Z%2FqPFqMK5wpFCRt3NunzF4UXqUty6R6XvhVxE3Un4%3D&reserved=0)identified 24 observational studies including 15,809 patients. PERT use was associated with lower in-hospital or 30-day mortality (OR 0.72, 95% CI 0.56–0.93), more frequent use of advanced therapies (OR 3.16, 95% CI 1.81–5.49), less major or clinically relevant bleeding (OR 0.60, 95% CI 0.42–0.86), and shorter hospital length of stay (mean difference −1.49 days, 95% CI −2.59 to −0.39), with no significant difference in 30-day readmission. The primary limitations of this meta-analysis were that all included studies were observational (hence at risk of [selection bias](https://nam10.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=http%3A%2F%2Fpmid.us%2F21491415&data=05%7C02%7Cnsang%40wustl.edu%7C4789d2d14f0f4646aefe08de8d0a04aa%7C4ccca3b571cd4e6d974b4d9beb96c6d6%7C0%7C0%7C639103272193224764%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=VHDB4ig9t12wQyB5QKbVh9Wa6VmYadJ8gMdBKg5qRgY%3D&reserved=0), [information bias](https://nam10.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fpmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov%2Farticles%2FPMC4862344%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cnsang%40wustl.edu%7C4789d2d14f0f4646aefe08de8d0a04aa%7C4ccca3b571cd4e6d974b4d9beb96c6d6%7C0%7C0%7C639103272193233300%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=EIg5iCSz47YcAYMkqClWwYhdgKeYeitqKgRnv8NJ%2FCU%3D&reserved=0), and [confounding](https://nam10.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fpmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov%2Farticles%2FPMC8786092%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cnsang%40wustl.edu%7C4789d2d14f0f4646aefe08de8d0a04aa%7C4ccca3b571cd4e6d974b4d9beb96c6d6%7C0%7C0%7C639103272193241635%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=RM%2BnQFfb7XKUR3Cdkens0%2BsfuOB64Fn803tWl4wGMI4%3D&reserved=0)) and that most outcomes showed substantial heterogeneity between studies (I² often > 60–90%).

Overall, PERT involvement in the management of intermediate-risk PE seems to improve outcomes, current evidence does not demonstrate clear-cut patient-centered outcome benefits for the alternative therapies offered. The primary limitations of studies on these therapies include potential bias from industry funding and the use of surrogate rather than patient-centered outcomes. Anticoagulation thus remains the standard of care, with selective use of advanced interventions and multidisciplinary PERT guidance in carefully chosen patients pending larger, high-quality trials focused on meaningful clinical outcomes.
